cards.title: Recognize anti-phishing images as a non-factor
cards.summary: A bank-style personal image shown before password entry does not defend the customer and is trivially relayed by an attacker in the middle; replace such theater with HTTPS plus a verifiable server credential.
cards.use_when: Reviewing branded or in-house authentication schemes on your site, or a vendor pitching a custom 'trust indicator' before login.

cards.title: Rate SMS and app-based one-time codes by interception and phishing risk
cards.summary: SMS and TOTP codes are interceptable and phishable in real time, so treat them as better-than-nothing second factors, not as strong authentication.
cards.use_when: Choosing the default 2FA method for shopper accounts, staff accounts, or a mandatory step at checkout.

cards.title: Use push-notification login, but read approval prompts carefully
cards.summary: Push approval avoids SMS-network risks and runs over secure transport, yet it remains phishable because the prompt is not cryptographically tied to the site the customer is visiting.
cards.use_when: Evaluating an authenticator-app or push-based login for shopper or admin accounts.

cards.title: Design account recovery before you enforce strong factors
cards.summary: Recovery is an unsolved problem: the more fallback flexibility you allow, the more of your strong-factor guarantees you give away, so decide the trade-off deliberately.
cards.use_when: Planning 2FA rollout for shopper accounts or choosing what the support desk may accept to unlock an account.

cards.title: Adopt hardware-backed sign-in and passwordless flows via the browser credential API
cards.summary: WebAuthn lets a customer register a credential (create) and then prove control of it (get), backing passwordless or username-less login with keys held in a hardware secure element.
cards.use_when: Choosing how to implement security-key or biometric login on your storefront and deciding between passwordless and password-plus-key.

cards.title: Choose between device-bound and synced credentials for shopkeeper and customer logins
cards.summary: A credential bound to one device's secure element cannot be used elsewhere without physical access, while synced credentials trade that assurance for recoverability across a customer's devices.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether storefront or back-office logins should require a specific physical key versus allowing biometrics synced through a platform account.

cards.title: Run authentication as a pluggable abstraction so you can adopt stronger credentials later
cards.summary: The source's core architectural argument is to abstract authentication behind a create/get interface so physical keys, biometrics, pins or passwords all sit behind the same site logic.
cards.use_when: Scoping authentication work on a new storefront or replatforming an existing account system.

cards.title: Check the WebAuthn, CTAP and U2F naming before integrating a device
cards.summary: The ecosystem's overlapping names (WebAuthn, FIDO2, CTAP, U2F) describe different layers, and mismatched support produces devices that simply do not work with a given browser.
cards.use_when: Evaluating security-key hardware or browser support while adding key-based login to a storefront.

cards.title: Handle credential-registration privacy between sites
cards.summary: A credential used on multiple sites should not let those sites correlate the same customer, though within a single site re-registering an existing key is intentionally detectable for usability.
cards.use_when: Reviewing whether your login implementation leaks user identity signals across your own properties or partner sites.

cards.title: Value QR-code cross-device login honestly
cards.summary: QR-based login links a phone to a desktop session and can be strong when the phone's own unlock and transport are secure, but the code is visible on screen and the flow is still phishable.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to offer scan-to-login on a storefront or in a merchant app.

cards.title: Treat client certificates and SSH keys as real factors in recovery
cards.summary: Client certificates and SSH keys can authenticate a customer or staff member even though they are not used to sign in to the website directly, and they are commonly accepted in recovery flows.
cards.use_when: Auditing ecommerce account-recovery and support processes, or assessing what an integration key can do if exposed.

cards.title: Separate authentication from authorization in the credential design
cards.summary: Proving who a user is and deciding what that user may do are different problems, and the credential protocol the source discusses only addresses the first.
cards.use_when: Scoping account-access requirements for a storefront, a merchant back office, or an agent that acts on a customer's behalf.

cards.title: Name the customer-facing credential plainly for storefront login
cards.summary: User-facing terminology for credentials is unsettled, and the source warns that device-centric wording now ambiguously means both an external key and the customer's own phone.
cards.use_when: Writing the account-security settings copy, login buttons and help articles for your storefront.

cards.title: Identify and Prioritize Node.js Core vs Dependency vs App Vulnerabilities
cards.summary: Separate vulnerabilities into three layers (core runtime, ecosystem packages/embedded deps, your own app) and treat each with its own patching and threat-model response so storefront fixes target the right layer.
cards.use_when: Planning a vulnerability review or patch cycle for an ecommerce storefront/backend running on Node.js, or deciding whether a scanner finding is your code, a package, or the runtime.

cards.title: Use CVE, CWE and CVSS as a Shared Vocabulary for Storefront Findings
cards.summary: Adopt MITRE's CVE/CWE databases and the CVSS calculator as a common language to catalog, describe and score vulnerabilities so your team can compare and prioritize store security findings consistently.
cards.use_when: Documenting or triaging a security finding in an ecommerce stack, or deciding how severely to treat a reported bug in your runtime or a package.

cards.title: Threat-Model Your Whole Domain, Not Just Your Software
cards.summary: Treat your entire external footprint — including DNS records and abandoned subdomains — as attack surface, using a real domain-takeover case as the model for finding non-code vulnerabilities.
cards.use_when: Auditing the security of your store's external estate (DNS, subdomains, marketing pages, CDN configuration) or setting up a threat-modeling exercise for your ecommerce operation.

cards.title: Never Expose Node Inspector/Debug Ports on Storefront Servers
cards.summary: Close and credential-protect debug ports like the Node inspector (e.g., port 5858) because internet scanners constantly probe them and exposure lets attackers gain full code execution on the host.
cards.use_when: Running or debugging a Node.js storefront or backend on a server, or reviewing server configuration for exposed management/debug endpoints.

cards.title: Design an Embargo and Coordinated-Disclosure Process for Security Findings
cards.summary: Keep vulnerability details strictly need-to-know until public disclosure, using time-bounded embargoes and staged notification so you can patch before attackers learn the vulnerability.
cards.use_when: Coordinating a fix for a known vulnerability in your store's stack, briefing contractors/vendors, or scoping who on your team can access a security finding before it is public.

cards.title: Set Explicit Response SLAs for Security Reports
cards.summary: Commit to and track concrete response times for incoming vulnerability reports so third-party researchers and your own team know what to expect and gaps become visible.
cards.use_when: Running a bug-report intake for your storefront, or setting expectations with a security researcher, agency, or bug-bounty platform.

cards.title: CSRF fundamentals: ambient cookie authority and forged state-changing requests
cards.summary: How cookie ambient authority lets attacker sites submit authenticated requests, and why storefront state-changing endpoints (cart, address, payment, admin) need explicit anti-CSRF protection.
cards.use_when: Auditing or designing any authenticated storefront action that changes state: add-to-cart, save address, place order, change email/password, refund, or admin config.

cards.title: Implement stateless CSRF tokens with HMAC over the session ID
cards.summary: Use an HMAC of the session ID with a server-only secret, instead of storing random per-user tokens, so any number of parallel sessions validate without server-side token storage.
cards.use_when: Building or reviewing the anti-CSRF token layer for a storefront or admin panel, especially when you need validation across many open tabs without server-side token state.

cards.title: Why the CSRF token defeats a forged request: same-origin policy blocks token theft
cards.summary: The CSRF token works because cross-site JavaScript cannot read the token out of your store's page DOM, so a forged request cannot echo it back even though cookies are attached.
cards.use_when: Explaining, debugging or threat-modeling why a suspicious request should be rejected on an ecommerce session, and validating a token defense behaves correctly.

cards.title: Validate the method, not just the token, in redirect/callback handlers
cards.summary: The GitHub OAuth CSRF bypass hinged on a single URL serving GET (render page) and POST (do action); storefront callbacks and payment returns should branch strictly on HTTP method and re-validate state.
cards.use_when: Designing or reviewing login-with-X, OAuth callbacks, payment-gateway return URLs, or any endpoint that both renders a page and performs a state change.

cards.title: Use threat modeling to choose controls, not just to list bugs
cards.summary: The node security roadmap shows how to systematically enumerate threats for your runtime environment, rate their severity and map solutions — adaptable to an ecommerce stack's threat environment.
cards.use_when: Defining the security posture for a new ecommerce platform, integration or checkout flow, or when deciding which threats warrant investment.

cards.title: npm install runs arbitrary code — isolate builds from production hosts
cards.summary: Because post-install scripts execute on every module, package installation is effectively remote code execution; build inside disposable isolation, not on a long-lived production VM.
cards.use_when: Setting up CI/CD or deployment processes for an ecommerce storefront or custom service, and deciding where dependencies get installed.

cards.title: Keep a live dependency inventory and patch systemically
cards.summary: Maintaining a known-current dependency inventory lets you find vulnerable packages, but the source warns audit tools alone won't catch everything.
cards.use_when: Running periodic dependency hygiene for an ecommerce platform or custom service, and deciding when to schedule patching.

cards.title: Supply-chain defense: network policy inside the build container
cards.summary: The event-stream Bitcoin-wallet attack demonstrates that source review is not enough; limiting a build container's egress to known domains can neutralize install-time payloads.
cards.use_when: Hardening the build pipeline for an ecommerce storefront or service that installs third-party packages.

cards.title: Never let security process strangle developer velocity
cards.summary: The source argues that overly rigid security process pushes people to route around it, which is itself a major vulnerability — balance control with pragmatic, staged gates.
cards.use_when: Designing or reforming the security review process for an ecommerce engineering team, especially when balancing shipping speed against compliance.

cards.title: Match your threat model to the hosting/runtime model you actually use
cards.summary: Serverless and managed runtimes move the patch burden to the provider but introduce a different threat — an attacker can drain your metered resources instead of taking you down.
cards.use_when: Choosing between self-managed VMs, containers and serverless for a storefront or service, and setting cost/abuse guardrails.

cards.title: Stability vs. security: when not to change a component (and what it costs)
cards.summary: The source describes holding a known-problematic legacy parser deployed because changing it could break timing assumptions in large systems — a trade-off reminder for storefront platform work.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to swap out a core dependency, parser or subsystem in a running ecommerce platform where behavior and timing matter.

cards.title: Recognize composite attacks and layered defenses
cards.summary: The source stresses that attackers chain several vulnerabilities together (e.g. an out-of-bounds write to turn a crash into escalation), so single-layer controls are insufficient.
cards.use_when: Reviewing the security posture of an ecommerce stack and deciding how to layer controls across application, runtime and infrastructure.

cards.title: Watch for slow, hard-to-detect degradation from abuse
cards.summary: The source describes slow-request attacks that gradually leak resources and degrade a service without obvious errors — monitoring should catch gradual decline, not just hard failures.
cards.use_when: Setting up monitoring and anomaly detection for an ecommerce backend, especially around request handling, checkout timeouts and resource exhaustion.

cards.title: Treat admin/integration endpoints as high-value attack surface
cards.summary: Every system that exposes authentication-adjacent endpoints (OAuth, SSO, webhooks, admin APIs) needs its own review; a fix in one interface does not automatically cover a legacy or parallel one.
cards.use_when: Reviewing storefront integration endpoints: login-with-provider flows, webhook receivers, admin APIs and any legacy interface still reachable.

cards.title: General server hardening for ecommerce stacks
cards.summary: A practical starter checklist drawn from the source's closing guidance on protecting a node-based service, adaptable to any storefront backend.
cards.use_when: Establishing baseline security hygiene for an ecommerce backend before launch or during periodic review.

cards.title: Prefer simple browser-level security over repeated per-app logic
cards.summary: The source argues CSRF tokens existed because browsers offered no built-in alternative; once a browser-level feature (SameSite) exists, prefer it because per-app logic is error-prone and easy to miss on one endpoint.
cards.use_when: Setting cookie attributes and session policy for a storefront, and deciding what security logic belongs in the browser vs your application code.

cards.title: Treat agent/tool instructions and retrieved documents as untrusted data
cards.summary: The source's supply-chain and injection themes translate to agent security: content a tool retrieves — including package manifests, web pages and API responses — must not be treated as authorization for agent actions.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing agents that operate on an ecommerce stack (listing changes, pricing updates, support replies) and consume external or user-supplied content.

cards.title: Security researcher case studies: read disclosed vulnerabilities as learning material
cards.summary: Platform vulnerability trackers and disclosure posts catalog real attack patterns (command injection in packages, SQL injection in ORMs) that you can translate into tests and controls for your own store.
cards.use_when: Building a security training or testing backlog for an ecommerce engineering team, and turning disclosed bugs into prevention checks.

cards.title: Avoid brittle input-parsing and URL handling in storefront code
cards.summary: The source catalogs parser bugs (out-of-bounds writes, URL/hostname spoofing, request splitting) as reminders that hand-rolled parsing of user input, URLs and headers is a recurring source of exploitable flaws.
cards.use_when: Reviewing custom parsing in storefront code: URL rewriting, redirect handling, header parsing, and any code that interprets user-supplied paths or hosts.

cards.title: Assign threat owners and triage routes before an incident
cards.summary: The source describes a triage model where ecosystem vulnerabilities were routed to third parties rather than the core project — clarify in advance who investigates what, so reports don't fall through.
cards.use_when: Setting up vulnerability intake and disclosure handling for an ecommerce platform team or a vendor it depends on.

cards.title: Method-specific routes prevent CSRF bypass via HEAD
cards.summary: Routing multiple HTTP methods to one handler hides an unvalidated third case (HEAD) that can skip CSRF checks entirely.
cards.use_when: Designing or reviewing storefront routes that handle form submissions, cart mutations, checkout actions, or any endpoint that changes account or order state.

cards.title: Fail fast when an assumption is violated
cards.summary: Crashing on unexpected states surfaces bugs immediately rather than continuing in an unknown, possibly corrupted state.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing server handlers for cart operations, order state transitions, or any multi-step process where a mid-step exception would leave inconsistent state.

cards.title: Fixleakyabstractions that hide security-relevant detail
cards.summary: An abstraction that leaks edge-case behavior (like HEAD behaving unlike GET) forces developers to know internals and breeds exploitable surprises.
cards.use_when: Choosing or building an ecommerce framework layer, integration SDK, or internal API that other code on your store depends on.

cards.title: Avoid APIs with insecure defaults or polymorphic signatures
cards.summary: Functions that are insecure by default or that do different things based on argument type/count are easy to misuse in security-critical code.
cards.use_when: Selecting a library or designing an internal helper (e.g., a data-encoding, password, or serialization utility) for your store's backend.

cards.title: Uninitialized-buffer disclosure: prevent leaking memory from user input
cards.summary: A benign-looking 'encode this string' endpoint became a memory-disclosure bug when a string parameter was swapped for a number.
cards.use_when: Reviewing any backend endpoint that turns user input into bytes, encodings, or binary data — e.g., image/thumbnail generation, PDF export, or a convert/encode utility in your store.

cards.title: Bind listeners to the intended interface
cards.summary: A server started without an explicit IP binds to all network interfaces, exposing it beyond localhost.
cards.use_when: Deploying or testing a store's backend, admin panel, or internal tool — especially during development before it goes behind a load balancer.

cards.title: Give checkout and admin API calls their own signed context
cards.summary: Each high-impact action (authorize app, change order, refund) should re-check authorization in the same code path that performs it.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing authorization for sensitive ecommerce operations like refunds, order edits, app/integration installs, or admin actions.

cards.title: Design-time checklist for reducing server complexity
cards.summary: Complexity is the common root cause of server security bugs; reduce it via explicit code, isolated components, and fail-fast checks.
cards.use_when: Architecture or code review for any store backend, especially before adding an integration or refactoring authentication/checkout code.

cards.title: Verify agent tool permissions and trust retrieved content as data only
cards.summary: Convert the lesson's 'never trust input' principle to AI agents: retrieved documents and tool output are untrusted data, not authorization.
cards.use_when: Configuring an agent that reads product feeds, customer reviews, support emails, or external APIs and can act on your store (edit listings, issue refunds, place orders).

cards.title: CSRF defense for storefront authenticated actions
cards.summary: How ambient cookie authority lets a third-party page trigger authenticated store actions, and how SameSite cookies or synchronizer tokens prevent it.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing protection for authenticated ecommerce actions that change state: placing an order on a saved card, editing addresses, changing subscription billing, adding admin products, or any log-in-with-X flow.

cards.title: CSRF token bypass via HTTP HEAD and framework magic
cards.summary: The GitHub OAuth bug: a route accepting GET and POST in one handler let HEAD requests skip the framework's POST-only CSRF check and auto-authorize an app.
cards.use_when: Reviewing route handlers, OAuth/SSO callbacks, or any endpoint that mixes HTTP methods, especially where an external integration can be auto-approved for a shopper or merchant account.

cards.title: Defensively whitelist HTTP methods in store endpoints
cards.summary: Treat unexpected HTTP methods as catastrophic: explicit else-if branches and hard aborts stop fall-through into sensitive store logic.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing route handlers for cart, checkout, subscription, account, or admin endpoints where method confusion could trigger an action a shopper did not intend.

cards.title: SameSite strict vs lax: don't break OAuth login on your storefront
cards.summary: Choosing SameSite Strict can break third-party OAuth/SSO logins and top-level redirects, so Lax is often required for storefront login flows.
cards.use_when: Configuring session cookie attributes for a store that uses 'Log in with Google/Twitter/X' or any third-party identity provider redirecting back into checkout.

cards.title: Leaky abstractions in frameworks cause security bugs
cards.summary: When a framework hides complexity imperfectly (like auto-handling HEAD as GET), developer assumptions break and security checks can be skipped.
cards.use_when: Evaluating framework conveniences when building storefront features, especially anything the framework implements 'for you' that touches method dispatch, auth, or CSRF.

cards.title: Defensive coding: assert assumptions and fail closed on sensitive actions
cards.summary: For high-value grants, validate the security check explicitly at the point of action and abort rather than recovering from violated assumptions.
cards.use_when: Implementing any endpoint that grants access or changes something valuable: linking a payment provider, adding an admin integration, approving an app, or changing payout/bank details on a merchant account.

cards.title: Split storefront routes by HTTP method and purpose
cards.summary: One URL handling both a read page and a state-changing submission is the structural factor that made the bypass possible; separate routes prevent it.
cards.use_when: Designing URL and route structure for storefront consent pages, integration authorization, subscription management, or any page that both renders a form and processes its submission.

cards.title: Governing agent and integration access with OAuth scopes
cards.summary: OAuth grant flows hand an app a token as powerful as the user's account, so scope minimization and consent scrutiny matter for store integrations.
cards.use_when: Authorizing third-party apps, marketing tools, or agents to act on a store (read orders, edit products, access customer data), or onboarding any OAuth-based integration into checkout/admin.

cards.title: Responding to reported vulnerabilities on your store
cards.summary: A clear report-to-fix loop and severity-based responsiveness limit damage from storefront and integration vulnerabilities.
cards.use_when: Setting up or triaging a vulnerability reporting process for a store, theme, app, or integration, especially for sites running your code or processing shopper data.

cards.title: Treat Leaky Abstractions as Likely Edge-Case Holes in Store Code
cards.summary: An abstraction that hides HTTP method details still forces developers to know them, so unmapped methods like HEAD slip through as unhandled cases.
cards.use_when: Reviewing or building shared ecommerce code (library, middleware, internal SDK) that wraps HTTP requests between storefront, checkout, fulfillment or third-party integrations.

cards.title: Reduce Component Interactions, Not Just Component Count
cards.summary: Security risk grows with how many things a new component can interact with, not just how many components you add.
cards.use_when: Scoping a new storefront integration, payment provider connection, fulfillment hook, or automation connector before adding it to the ecommerce stack.

cards.title: Use Explicit Code Over Clever Code in Security-Relevant Paths
cards.summary: Verbose, dumb-looking code you can still understand months later is safer than a clever one-liner no one can audit.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing checkout, auth, payment or PII-handling code where future maintainers must be able to verify behavior.

cards.title: Fail Early on Unexpected State; Handle Expected Errors Gracefully
cards.summary: Crash on exceptions you didn't anticipate, but return normal error responses for errors your code explicitly expects.
cards.use_when: Deciding how a store's server should behave when errors occur — e.g., product lookups, cart operations, payment callbacks.

cards.title: Assume Inputs Are Wrong: Verify Assumptions at the Top of Each Function
cards.summary: Code defensively by validating function arguments and request data up front rather than assuming they match what you expect.
cards.use_when: Building any store endpoint or handler — product search, discount application, admin actions — that trusts request parameters.

cards.title: Reject APIs Whose Insecure Path Is the Easy Path
cards.summary: If a function only works securely when you pass a pile of options, most callers will be insecure by default.
cards.use_when: Choosing or wrapping third-party libraries and SDKs for a store — payment processors, auth providers, encryption helpers, bot-defense tools.

cards.title: Watch for Hidden Behavioral Switches in Function Signatures
cards.summary: Some frameworks change a function's entire behavior based on argument count, so an 'unused' argument can be load-bearing.
cards.use_when: Reviewing or refactoring middleware, hooks or plugin functions in a store's web framework where behavior depends on signature shape.

cards.title: Secure Binary/Buffer Encoding Endpoints Against Memory Disclosure
cards.summary: Constructing a buffer from a numeric input can allocate uninitialized memory and return stale process data, including secrets.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing any store endpoint that handles binary data, encoding/conversion, or user-supplied buffer-like inputs.

cards.title: Never Bind Servers to All Interfaces by Default
cards.summary: A listen call without an explicit address can expose the service to every machine that can reach the host.
cards.use_when: Deploying or configuring any store service — API, admin panel, internal tool — where bind address and exposure matter.

cards.title: Add CSRF Validation Centrally for State-Changing Requests
cards.summary: Route-wide middleware that checks CSRF tokens on state-changing methods is the pattern the source cites for validating requests globally.
cards.use_when: Securing store forms and state-changing endpoints — checkout submission, cart mutation, account changes, admin actions.

cards.title: Use Strongly Typed Checks to Force Exhaustive Case Handling
cards.summary: A compiler that errors on unhandled cases prevents the class of bug where a developer handles only some input variants.
cards.use_when: Choosing languages or tooling for store components that branch on request type, payment status or order state where missing a case is costly.

cards.title: Treat memory disclosure and uninitialized buffers as a storefront data-leak risk
cards.summary: A no-op server can leak past-request memory if it serializes buffers naively, so bound and clear any response that echoes user data.
cards.use_when: Building or reviewing any storefront endpoint, agent tool, or middleware that returns request data, error dumps, or templated responses back to a browser.

cards.title: User interaction before a sensitive local or remote action
cards.summary: Requiring an explicit click before performing a state-changing action neutralizes most drive-by request attacks, even when the endpoint accepts them.
cards.use_when: Designing storefront or admin features that a browser could trigger without the customer's intent, such as store locators, device pairing, card-on-file actions, or integration callbacks.

cards.title: Use non-simple requests as a defense in depth, not as the fix
cards.summary: Requiring a preflighted method or custom header stops cross-site simple requests, but DNS rebinding and non-browser clients bypass it.
cards.use_when: Hardening a local or internal HTTP endpoint (device gateway, integration listener, admin service) that currently accepts simple GET/POST requests.

cards.title: Scope local-network and integration endpoints so a browser cannot reach them
cards.summary: A privileged listener that accepts requests from any page reachable by the customer's browser is a cross-site path into the local network or the store's internal services; bind it to the required origin or protocol instead.
cards.use_when: Deploying device gateways, print/label services, POS bridges, or any ecommerce integration listener that runs on a store machine or local network.

cards.title: Capabilities of a same-origin rebinding-style attack on storefronts
cards.summary: A page that appears same-origin can bypass cross-origin restrictions and firewalls to reach local and internal services, which matters for IOT devices, printers, and admin tooling around ecommerce operations.
cards.use_when: Assessing risk when store systems, fulfillment hardware, or admin consoles share a network with the customer's or staff's browsing environment.

cards.title: Keep access-control headers off endpoints that never meant to share data
cards.summary: An overly permissive Access-Control-Allow-Origin on a local or internal endpoint lets any site read the response even when it cannot be prevented from sending the request.
cards.use_when: Reviewing CORS configuration on local services, internal tooling, or storefront APIs that return customer, order, or token data.

cards.title: Use allowlist identity keys and reject unauthenticated state changes
cards.summary: The source's thermostat example shows the core failure mode: a device or endpoint accepting unauthenticated GETs from anywhere on the network, which any page or integration can exploit.
cards.use_when: Reviewing connected device integrations, IoT hardware, or admin endpoints that control physical or financial state in a store or customer environment.

cards.title: Simple vs preflighted requests: which cross-site calls a page can make
cards.summary: Only requests expressible in plain HTML (GET, form POST with limited content types, no custom headers) can be sent cross-origin without a permission check; everything else triggers a preflight that the server can refuse.
cards.use_when: Deciding which storefront or integration endpoint methods a hostile page could reach, and designing the method/content-type/header profile accordingly.

cards.title: Treat agent- and browser-initiated requests as untrusted input, not authorization
cards.summary: A retrieved page, document, or tool response is data: it can carry instructions that look authoritative, so it must never by itself authorize an agent or page to perform store actions.
cards.use_when: Building checkout helpers, admin copilots, or automation that reads pages, emails, tickets, or vendor docs and can act on the store's systems.

cards.title: Give each listener its own port and verify the actual request on the wire
cards.summary: Demo and production setups often break because two services share a port or because the browser sends a preflight instead of the intended method; check the network tab rather than the page's apparent behavior.
cards.use_when: Debugging or reviewing an integration listener, local gateway, or webhook receiver that appears to accept requests but behaves unexpectedly.

cards.title: Hostname-to-IP reassociation is the mechanism to explain in store risk reviews
cards.summary: An origin is scheme+hostname+port, with no binding to the underlying IP, so a hostname that controls its own DNS answers can shift to point at a local or internal address without changing origin.
cards.use_when: Briefing engineers or vendors on why origin checks and allowlists alone do not protect local services, integrations, or connected devices in a store environment.

cards.title: Validate the mitigation against non-browser callers too
cards.summary: Browser-enforced controls (preflight, same-origin, read restrictions) are executed by the browser only, so any native script or service on the machine bypasses them entirely.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether an endpoint is actually safe when the threat model includes admin tooling, scripts, mobile apps, third-party integrations, or local automation.
